extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and aesthetics (readers of Kant)
extracted.subtask_short: aesthetic evaluation of art and beauty
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and distinctions for judging beauty, art, genius, and taste in aesthetic philosophy — how to evaluate/produce beautiful objects and artworks according to Kantian aesthetics. Includes distinctions between natural vs. artificial beauty, pleasant vs. beautiful art, and the faculties required for judgement and production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness of the Judgment of Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: That is beautiful which pleases in the mere act of judging it (not in the sensation of it, or by means of a concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pleasure must arise from the act of reflective judgement itself rather than from sensible enjoyment or from a determinate concept (purpose). This disinterested pleasure is the mark of a pure aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal Communicability of Aesthetic Pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The universal communicability of a pleasure carries with it that the pleasure is derived from reflection; aesthetical art has for standard the reflective judgement and not sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic judgements claim a form of universal validity (we expect others to share the pleasure) even though they are not founded on objective concepts. This communicability distinguishes aesthetic standards from mere private sensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate Intellectual Interest in Natural Beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: To take an immediate interest in the beauty of Nature (not merely to have taste in judging it) is always a mark of a good soul and indicates a frame of mind favourable to moral feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate interest is exemplified by someone who delights in a wild flower or bird for its presence alone (no advantage sought). If the object is discovered to be artificial (e.g., planted fake flowers or a carved bird), this immediate interest disappears — demonstrating the requirement that nature must have produced the beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Immediate and Mediate Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: An interest bound up with beauty can be immediate (intrinsic to the object, especially natural beauty) or mediate (referable to social advantage or vanity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate interest is disinterested and may link to moral feeling; mediate interest is empirical and allied to inclination (e.g., vanity, social esteem). Mediate interests do not reliably indicate moral disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasant Art vs Beautiful Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasant arts are directed merely to enjoyment (sensible pleasure); beautiful art is a mode of representation purposive for itself and furthers the culture of the mental powers in reference to social communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasant arts (entertaining stories, convivial music, games) aim at momentary sensory enjoyment. Beautiful art aims at reflective satisfaction, communicability, and cultivation — its standard is reflective judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness without Purpose (Art must 'look' purposive but without obvious design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful art must be purposive for itself though devoid of definite purpose; its purposiveness must not seem designed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work of art should appear free from constraint and not show the obtrusive presence of rules; the design must not be painfully apparent. This 'as-if-natural' purposiveness enables the universally communicable pleasure of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful Art Should Seem Like Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: For art to be beautiful it must be art (we must be conscious that it is art) yet its form must seem as free and purposive as if produced by nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The product must not betray the mechanical schooling or the rule-following that produced it. Example anti-pattern: the form of schools obtruding itself so that the rule is painfully apparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art Distinguished from Nature (production through freedom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is production through freedom (facere) distinct from natural action (agere); art presupposes a will that places Reason at the basis of its actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objects are called art when their producing cause conceived a purpose. Natural regularities (e.g., bees' cells) are analogically called art only if one forgets lack of rational deliberation in the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art Distinguished from Science
rubrics_metrics.description: Art (practical faculty, technic) differs from science (theoretical faculty); knowing what ought to be done is not the same as having the skill to do it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One can describe how to make something (science) without possessing the capacity (art) to execute it — example: Camper can describe best shoe-making but may not make one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art Distinguished from Handicraft (free vs mercenary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art regarded as human skill differs from handicraft: the first is free (playful, pleasant in itself), the second mercenary (work, unpleasant except for its effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free arts are occupations pleasant in themselves; handicrafts are occupations carried out for wages. The distinction can be context-dependent (e.g., professional hierarchies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical Art vs Aesthetical (Beautiful) Art
rubrics_metrics.description: If art performs actions merely to make a possible object actual, it is mechanical; if it has for its immediate design the feeling of pleasure (as a mode of cognition), it is aesthetical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical art aims at useful production; aesthetical art aims at reflective pleasure. Beautiful art requires both genius (for originality) and a mechanical element (rules, craft) for execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius as Source of Beautiful Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is the innate mental disposition through which Nature gives the rule to Art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties of genius: (1) originality (talent for producing that for which no definite rule can be given); (2) produces exemplary models, not imitable precepts; (3) cannot fully explain or teach its own process; (4) prescribes rules to art (not to science). Genius is necessary for beautiful art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius Opposed to Imitation and Not Teachability
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is entirely opposed to the spirit of imitation; the capacity of teachableness (learning by imitation) is not the ground of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific discoveries can be taught in sequence; artistic genius cannot be conveyed by rules or precepts. Anti-pattern: confusing great learnable skill with genius (e.g., Newton vs Homer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Models as Rules for Art (rule abstracted from product)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule of genius cannot be given as a formula; it must be abstracted from the product — models of beautiful art serve as standards for imitation (not copyable precepts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists' models excite like ideas in pupils endowed with similar faculties; instruction by description is insufficient for beautiful arts (especially speech/poetry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste vs Genius (judging vs producing)
rubrics_metrics.description: For judging beautiful objects as such, taste is requisite; for producing such objects (beautiful art), genius is requisite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taste is a judging (not productive) faculty, trained by examples; genius is the productive innate talent. Artists need both: genius for original material, cultivated taste/skill for execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of Disgust Cannot Be Beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one kind of ugliness which cannot be represented in accordance with nature without destroying all aesthetical satisfaction: that which excites disgust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While art can represent dreadful or calamitous subjects (Furies, war, disease) as beautiful, direct representations that provoke visceral disgust thwart the aesthetic distance required for beauty and thus fail as beautiful art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetical Ideas and 'Spirit' as Animating Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Spirit (in an aesthetical sense) is the animating principle of the mind manifested by the faculty of presenting aesthetical Ideas: representations of the Imagination which occasion much thought without any definite concept being adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetical Ideas (e.g., poetic visions of eternity, creation, love, death) stimulate imagination beyond empirical limits and cannot be exhaustively captured by concepts — this faculty supplies 'spirit' to works of art and is especially manifest in poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination as a Creative Faculty Approximating Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The Imagination (as a productive faculty of cognition) remoulds experience in accordance with analogical laws and higher principles of Reason, thereby creating another nature and bringing intellectual Ideas into movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative imagination produces representations (Ideas/attributes) that strive beyond empirical experience, giving the appearance of objective reality to rational Ideas and thereby enriching the concept aesthetically.
